chapter: Learning from players; Jonah Jones lessons
title: Learning from other trumpeters; Roy Eldridge's chili and practice
summary: Maxwell urges pupils to listen rather than put others down and recalls Roy's morning practice.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him

blocks.x: Yeah. It's funny, you know, how -- I often tell pupils this kind of thing and they'll put down other musicians. They don't want to work in a band, this musician's bad. So I sort of sound like Will Rogers, but it's the truth, I've never met a trumpet player who can't do something I can't do, you know. And not one of those guys who can do something I can't do is not perfectly happy to tell you exactly what it is, you know. And you can learn a hell of a lot. Instead of putting down the guy sitting next to you, listen to him. Because you're going to find one thing he does pretty good, and you get him into a conversation, you know, how do you do this and that, and he's delighted to tell you how, you know. He'll give you a whole lesson. And I've learned so much from guys like that. You know, naturally from Cootie and Red Allen I learned a lot. And I used to go up and visit Roy -- I never knew that guys really practiced jazz solos until I met Roy and Ben Webster.

I'd go up to there place in the morning or something. Roy used to live -- I think it was Edgecombe Avenue. He had a pot full of chili, which I think he lived on. I don't think he ever ate anything but chili, morning, noon and night. And he would start practicing about 10:00 in the morning and he would just start in on a piece. And he would just play this piece everyway he could. Not that he worked his solos out, but he would just play and --
